heading: Sun, wind and the qulliq
intro: Indigenous nations and organizations in Edmonton, across Alberta and in Inuit Nunangat are building, owning and naming energy systems. Each one can be drawn like the systems in this lab: energy comes in from the surroundings, moves within the system and goes out. These connections use the names that nations themselves have given, with a source for each name.

connections.title: kīsikāw pīsim: daylight sun in the river valley
connections.text: Beside Edmonton's E.L. Smith Water Treatment Plant, EPCOR's solar farm uses 30,350 solar panels to turn sunlight into electricity. EPCOR says the farm makes more than 20,000 megawatt hours of energy each year. In 2022 Enoch Cree Nation gifted the farm its Cree name, kīsikāw pīsim, which EPCOR says means "daylight sun." The farm is in the city's sipiwiyiniwak ward. The City says sipiwiyiniwak means the River Cree, a name Enoch Cree Nation members were known by because they lived close to the river. Chief Billy Morin said the name acknowledges EPCOR's desire "to steward these lands."

sources.title: EPCOR: EPCOR officially opens the kīsikāw pīsim solar farm (30,350 panels; name gifted by Enoch Cree Nation in 2022)

Source of the name sipiwiyiniwak (the River Cree): City of Edmonton, Transforming Edmonton

peoples: Dene: K’ai Tailé Dené (Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation)
connections.title: Fort Chipewyan: sunlight in, less diesel
connections.text: Fort Chipewyan, in Treaty 8 territory, is not connected to Alberta's main power grid. CBC reports its diesel power station burned three million litres of fuel a year, trucked in on ice roads or brought by river barge. In 2020 Three Nations Energy opened a 2.2 MW solar farm there. It is owned by the Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation, who call themselves K’ai Tailé Dené, "people of the land of the willow," the Mikisew Cree First Nation and the Fort Chipewyan Métis Association. CBC reports it should replace about 800,000 litres of diesel a year. Mikisew Cree Chief Peter Powder said: "we're switching over to renewable energy."

sources.title: CBC News: Indigenous-owned solar farm opens in remote northern Alberta community (owners, 2.2 MW, diesel figures, quotes)

Source of the name K’ai Tailé Dené (people of the land of the willow) and of Treaty 8 signed at Fort Chipewyan in 1899: Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation, About Us

connections.title: Tarquti: tending energy in Nunavik
connections.text: Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami calls Inuit Nunangat the Inuit homeland in Canada, including Nunavik in Northern Quebec. Makivvik says all of Nunavik's electricity is produced by diesel generators. Tarquti Energy, which Makivvik says will be 100% Inuit-owned, aims to "allow Inuit to control the long-term development of renewable energy in Nunavik." Nunatsiaq News explains that a tarquti is the tool used to tend to a qulliq, the traditional oil lamp. In Iqaluit, Alacie Joamie said, "We survived because of the qulliq," the most reliable way to make heat while hunting and camping. Hydro-Québec says Tarquti's planned wind projects would supply about 60% of the electricity needs of Quaqtaq and Puvirnituq.

sources.title: Source of the names Inuit Nunangat (the Inuit homeland in Canada) and Nunavik: Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, Inuit Nunangat Map

Source of the name qulliq (traditional oil lamp) and Alacie Joamie's words: Nunatsiaq News, Iqaluit residents gather for an elder's qulliq lesson

try: Draw an energy transfer diagram with the kīsikāw pīsim solar farm and the water treatment plant together as one system. What energy comes in from the surroundings, what moves within, and what goes out? Now move the boundary so the system is only the plant. Which arrow now crosses the boundary?

One kilowatt hour is 3 600 000 J, so one megawatt hour is 3 600 000 000 J. Change EPCOR's "more than 20,000 megawatt hours" a year into joules. Then use the Fort Chipewyan numbers: if the station burned three million litres of diesel a year and the solar farm replaces about 800,000, about what fraction of the fuel coming into the power station's account is no longer needed?

Make a qulliq your system. Name its components, the energy that comes in with the fuel, and where energy goes out to the surroundings. As the oil burns, does the energy of the system go up or down? Then look at a wind turbine in Quaqtaq: where is a force moving something, so that work is done?

slide.notes: Use with Lesson 2 (Systems and surroundings) and Lesson 5 (Energy transfer diagrams). Ask students to choose a system boundary for one of the three examples and name the energy coming in and going out. The Fort Chipewyan numbers also suit Lesson 4 (Energy in, energy out) and the kWh row of the joule ladder. Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts.

review_flags: Existing content: I found no Indigenous content in the Energy Accounts Lab or the deck, sourced or unsourced. The lab's Edmonton examples (a house in January, the river valley cyclist, toboggan) have no Indigenous references.

Names used and where each comes from: kīsikāw pīsim, "daylight sun" (EPCOR solar farm page and media release; Windspeaker instead translates it "day sun," so I followed EPCOR); sipiwiyiniwak, "the River Cree" (City of Edmonton, Transforming Edmonton); K’ai Tailé Dené, "people of the land of the willow" (Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation's own About Us page); Inuit Nunangat and Nunavik (ITK); tarquti and qulliq (Nunatsiaq News). Quaqtaq, Puvirnituq, Iqaluit and Makivvik appear in sources, but none I fetched gave their meanings, so I gave no translations. I did not find a Cree name with a sourced meaning for Fort Chipewyan or for Mikisew; Mikisew Cree First Nation says its name honours Chief Mikisew (Justin Marten), Treaty 8 adhesion signatory, but gives no translation. I wrote "Cree" rather than nêhiyaw in the peoples fields because no source I fetched this session gives nêhiyaw. Do you want nêhiyaw added with a source?

kīsikāw pīsim is owned by EPCOR, not by Enoch Cree Nation. The Indigenous connection is the gifted name and the nation's relationship with the land. Windspeaker reports Chief Morin saying the land was taken from Enoch Cree Nation by the federal government in 1908, and that the name was presented through a pipe ceremony. I left both out on purpose (the ceremony is not mine to describe; the land history may need context from the nation). Should the land history be included, with Enoch Cree Nation's own words?

Fort Chipewyan numbers differ between sources: CBC gives 2.2 MW, 5,760 panels (6,000 in a caption), about 800,000 litres of diesel a year replaced and about 25 per cent of energy needs; CTV gives 6,000 panels and says the plant uses about five million litres a year; the 2019 NRCan release gave 650,000 litres and 20 per cent for the planned system. I used only CBC's numbers and avoided the panel count. Is that acceptable, or should I seek a Three Nations Energy statement? I could not find a 3NE website.
The Métis partner is named "Fort Chipewyan Métis Association" by CBC and CTV but "Fort Chipewyan Métis Local 125" by Natural Resources Canada (2019). Which name does the community use now?

Canada connection: Makivvik's statement that 100% of Nunavik's electricity comes from diesel is undated and may be outdated (a run of river project at Inukjuak is mentioned by Nunatsiaq News). Should I soften it to "Makivvik has said"? Also, Tarquti's ownership is described as 51 per cent Ilagiisaq (FCNQ) and 49 per cent Makivik in Nunatsiaq News (2021); I used Makivvik's "100% Inuit-owned" wording.

The qulliq is a living Inuit practice and its lighting is part of many gatherings. I only say what the lamp is and quote Alacie Joamie (Iqaluit, 2015, speaking in Inuktitut with translation by Leesee Papatsie). Nunatsiaq calls the session an elder's lesson; I did not add the title Elder to her name. Would you like to invite an Inuit Knowledge Keeper (for example through an Edmonton Inuit organization) to share about the qulliq rather than relying on a news article? The later Temperature and Heating lab may be a better home for any deeper qulliq content.
The try prompt about the qulliq asks students to treat it as a system. Please confirm this framing is respectful; an alternative is to keep the system prompts to the solar and wind projects only.

I did not use traditional technologies such as the bow drill, Red River cart, travois or qamutik because I did not find a reliable source in this session that describes them in terms of work or energy. A Métis Nation of Alberta solar farm (CBC, "A gift from the sun") appeared in search results but I did not fetch or use it; it could be a fourth connection or a Métis focused replacement if you want one.
